title: San Francisco health centers against national figures
question: For the federally supported health centers based in San Francisco, how do reported screening rates and cost per patient compare with health centers nationally?
finding: 7 health centers and look-alikes based in San Francisco filed a federal report for 2025. Nationally, health centers screened 45% of eligible adults for colorectal cancer and screened 75% of patients for depression with a follow-up plan; 6 of the 7 San Francisco centers were below the national figure on at least one of the two, led by Asian & Pacific Islander Wellness Center (25% and 53%). Where cost is published, the middle San Francisco center spent $4,205 per patient (3 centers), against $3,369 at 7 other Bay Area centers.
how: Each center's 2025 Uniform Data System report gives patients, total cost and, for each clinical quality measure, the number of patients who should have received a service and the number who did. The national figure is every reporting center's numerator added up and divided by every denominator. City money is everything the City paid the organization in fiscal year 2025, shown for scale only. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, less the payments it labels as loans, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. That figure includes money passing through: subsidies and insurance premiums that an organization pays on to others, and assessments that the City collects for a district and hands over. These are real City payments but not payment for the organization's own work. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made.
limits: These are the centers' own reports in a federal standard form, reviewed but not audited by the federal agency: they are the organization's account, not an outside count, and are treated that way in the verdicts below. Centers that mainly serve homeless people, people who use drugs or people with HIV see patients who are harder to screen, so a low rate is not a like-for-like comparison. National cost figures are not in the files saved here; cost per patient is compared with other Bay Area centers and is withheld for several centers.
